description: LUMORA hand-written seed intents (54). build_dataset.py merges mapped mid-term patterns and augments these into intents_augmented.json. Responses are non-diagnostic self-help guidance.

responses: Hi, I'm Lumora 💜 How are you feeling today?
Hello! I'm glad you're here. What's on your mind?
Hey there. How has your day been so far?
Take care of yourself. I'm here whenever you want to talk again. 💜
Goodbye for now. Be gentle with yourself today.
See you soon. Remember to rest and drink some water.

patterns: that makes me feel better, thanks
responses: You're very welcome. I'm glad that helped a little.
Thank you for trusting me with this. I'm here anytime.
I'm glad we talked. Is there anything else on your mind?
I'm Lumora, a supportive wellbeing chatbot made as a student project. I'm not a person, therapist or doctor, and I can't diagnose anything — but I can listen and share self-help ideas.
I'm Lumora 💜 — a chatbot that offers a safe space to talk, plus tools like mood tracking, journaling and mindfulness. For medical concerns, please see a professional.

patterns: i want to talk to someone
responses: I can listen, suggest coping ideas for stress, sleep, exams and relationships, guide breathing or grounding exercises, and point you to journaling, mood tracking and self-checks. What's been on your mind?
I'm here to talk things through with you. You can tell me how you feel, ask for coping tips, or try a mindfulness exercise. Where would you like to start?
Great. Take it slowly — small steps count.
Okay. Let me know how it goes, and we can adjust from there.
Sounds good. I'm here if you want to talk it through as you go.
Thanks for telling me — I may have misunderstood. Could you say a little more about what you need right now?
That's fair. Not every idea fits everyone. What has helped you even a little in the past?
I'm sorry that wasn't helpful. Let's try another angle — what feels hardest at the moment?
That's really lovely to hear! What do you think helped today feel good?
I'm so glad you're feeling this way. It might be nice to note it in your journal so you can look back on it.
That's wonderful. Celebrating good moments matters too — well done.

patterns: i'm under a lot of stress
i feel tense all the time
how do i deal with stress
i'm feeling a lot of pressure
my stress level is very high
responses: When stress builds up, it helps to slow your body down first: try breathing in for 4 counts and out for 6, a few times. Then pick just one thing to handle next.
Stress often feels smaller once it's written down. Try listing what's on your mind, then circle the one thing you can act on today.
A short break can reset your nervous system — a 10-minute walk, some water, or stretching your shoulders and neck.

patterns: i'm so anxious all the time
i feel nervous for no reason
my anxiety is really bad today
i have a constant feeling of dread
my heart races when i worry
how do i calm my anxiety
responses: Anxiety can make the body feel unsafe even when you are safe. Try the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding exercise: name 5 things you see, 4 you can touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell and 1 you taste.
Slow breathing helps calm anxious feelings: breathe in through your nose for 4, hold for 2, and breathe out slowly for 6. Repeat for a minute.
It can help to separate worries you can act on from ones you can't. For the ones you can, choose one small step; for the others, try setting a short daily 'worry time'.

patterns: i think i'm having a panic attack
i can't breathe properly and my heart is racing
my chest feels tight and i'm scared
i feel like i'm losing control
i'm shaking and can't calm down
i had a panic attack in class
how do i stop a panic attack
my hands are shaking and my heart is pounding
responses: You're not alone in this, and panic does pass. Try breathing out slowly, longer than you breathe in — in for 4, out for 6. Press your feet into the floor and name 5 things you can see. If you have chest pain or it doesn't ease, please seek medical help.

Let's slow things down together: put one hand on your chest, breathe in gently for 4, and out for 6. Notice something cold or textured you can touch. The wave of panic usually peaks and then fades within minutes.

patterns: i've been feeling down for days
responses: Low days are really hard. Something small and kind can help — a shower, sunlight for a few minutes, or messaging someone you trust. If this low mood lasts for weeks, talking to a professional is a good step.
It's okay not to be okay. Try doing one tiny thing you usually enjoy, even if you don't feel like it — mood often follows action, not the other way round.
Writing down what's weighing on you can make it feel a little lighter. Would a short journaling prompt help?

patterns: i have no one to talk to
responses: Loneliness is painful, and it's more common than it seems. A small reach-out — a message to an old friend or classmate — can be a first step back to connection.

Joining something regular, like a club, a study group or a volunteering activity, can make connection easier because you see the same people again. The anonymous Community page here is another gentle place to start.
Even short, low-pressure contact counts — chatting with a family member or saying hello to a neighbour. What kind of connection do you miss most?

patterns: my anger is out of control
responses: Anger is a signal that something matters to you. Before reacting, try stepping away for a few minutes and breathing out slowly; then name what triggered it.
Physical movement can release angry energy safely — a brisk walk, push-ups, or squeezing a pillow. Once calmer, you can decide how you want to respond.
Writing an 'unsent letter' can help: put everything you feel on paper, without sending it. Then notice what you actually need from the situation.

patterns: everything is too much right now
i have too much to do
i don't know where to start
i can't keep up with everything
i can't cope with everything at once
responses: When everything feels like too much, shrink the next step. Write down every task, then choose only the one that matters most for today.
Try a 'brain dump': list everything in your head for two minutes. Then sort it into 'today', 'this week' and 'can wait'.
Pause first. Take three slow breaths, drink some water, and then pick one small task you can finish in 15 minutes.

patterns: i worry about what will happen
i'm afraid i'll fail at life
i'm scared and don't know what to do
i fear i won't get a job
i'm worried all the time about tomorrow
pachi k huncha bhanera dar lagcha
responses: Worries about the future often feel certain even though they aren't. Try asking: what is in my control today? Then take one small step on that.
It may help to write the worst case, the best case and the most likely case. The most likely case is usually much more manageable.
Grounding yourself in the present can ease future-worry: notice your breath, your feet on the floor, and what's around you right now.

patterns: i hurt someone and feel terrible
i feel like a bad person
responses: Guilt can be a sign that you care about doing right. If you can, consider what repair might look like — an apology or a small kind act — and then practise forgiving yourself.
Try talking to yourself the way you'd talk to a close friend who made the same mistake. What would you say to them?
Separating the action from your worth helps: you made a mistake, but you are not a mistake. What did you learn that you'd do differently?

patterns: i feel jealous of my friends
everyone is doing better than me
i keep comparing myself to others
social media makes me feel bad about my life
my friend got what i wanted
why is everyone else so successful
i feel behind compared to my classmates
others have a better life than me
sabai jana malai bhanda agadi chan
responses: Comparison usually shows us someone else's highlights next to our hardest moments. Try comparing yourself only with who you were a month ago.
Jealousy can point to something you want. What is it showing you that you'd like for yourself? That can become a goal instead of a hurt.
A short break from social media, even for a day, often eases the comparison trap. Notice how you feel afterwards.

patterns: i don't enjoy my hobbies now
i don't feel like doing anything fun
i lost interest in things i used to like
responses: When interest fades, starting tiny helps — five minutes of a hobby, a new song, or a short walk somewhere different. If loss of interest lasts for weeks, it's worth talking to a professional.
Try something with a small sense of achievement, like tidying a drawer or cooking a simple meal. Small wins can spark energy.
Novelty can help: a different route home, a new podcast, or learning one small skill this week.

patterns: i feel tired all the time
i can't get out of bed
my body feels heavy and tired
i feel weak and tired every day
responses: Constant tiredness can come from poor sleep, stress, skipped meals or not enough movement. Try short breaks, staying hydrated and getting some daylight. If it continues, a doctor can check for physical causes.
Your body may be asking for rest. A 15–20 minute nap, gentle stretching or a quiet walk can help without ruining your night's sleep.
When energy is low, lower the bar: choose the most important task and let the rest wait.

patterns: i keep crying for no reason
i cried in the bathroom at college
i feel very emotional and sensitive
responses: Crying is a natural way your body releases emotion — it's okay. Let it happen, then try a glass of water and a few slow breaths.
It sounds like a lot has built up. After crying, gentle comfort helps: a warm drink, a blanket, or talking to someone you trust.
If it helps, you can tell me what brought the tears on. Sometimes naming the feeling makes it a little easier to hold.

patterns: i can't stop thinking about it
i replay conversations in my head
i keep thinking about what people think of me
i can't switch off my brain
responses: Overthinking often loses power on paper. Try writing the thought down, then ask: is this a problem I can solve now? If not, set it aside for a planned 'worry time'.
When thoughts loop, shift attention to your senses for a minute — what can you hear, see and feel right now?
Ask yourself: what's the evidence for this thought, and what's the evidence against it? Often a kinder, more balanced view appears.

patterns: my exams are coming and i'm scared
i have an exam tomorrow and i'm nervous
i'm not prepared for my exam
i'm afraid i'll fail my exams
board exams are making me anxious
i can't stop worrying about my results
responses: Exam stress is very common. Break revision into 25-minute focused blocks with 5-minute breaks, and start with the topics most likely to come up.
The night before an exam, sleep usually helps more than late cramming. Review key points, prepare your things, and do a few slow breaths before bed.
In the exam, if you blank out, pause, breathe out slowly, and start with a question you find easier to build momentum.

patterns: my parents will be angry about my result
i got back my result and i feel useless
i scored less than my friends
responses: A disappointing result hurts, but it doesn't define your ability or your future. When you feel ready, look at what went wrong and what you could change next time.
Many people recover from a bad result — retakes, different study methods and support from teachers can make a real difference. Who could you ask for guidance?
It might help to plan how to talk to your family: share the result, what you'll do differently, and the support you need.

patterns: my mind wanders when i study
i read but nothing goes in
i keep checking my phone while studying
how can i improve my concentration
i can't remember what i study
i lose focus after a few minutes
responses: Try the Pomodoro method: 25 minutes of focused study with your phone in another room, then a 5-minute break. Repeat four times, then take a longer break.
Active recall helps memory: after reading a section, close the book and write or say what you remember.
A tidy space, water nearby and a clear goal for each session ('finish 10 questions') can make focusing easier.

patterns: i leave everything to the last minute
i know i should study but i don't
i scroll on my phone instead of working
responses: Try the 2-minute rule: commit to just two minutes of the task. Starting is usually the hardest part, and momentum often follows.
Make the first step tiny and specific — not 'study biology', but 'read page 12'. Small, clear steps reduce the urge to delay.
Procrastination is often about avoiding a feeling, like fear of failing. Naming that feeling can make the task less scary.

patterns: how do i manage my time
i can't balance study and work
i never finish my tasks on time
how do i plan my day
responses: Try planning tomorrow tonight: list three priority tasks and give each a time slot. Anything extra is a bonus.
Block your time — study, rest, meals and sleep — so breaks are planned, not guilty. A realistic plan beats a perfect one.
Use the urgent/important split: do urgent and important first, schedule important but not urgent, and drop what's neither.

patterns: my parents expect too much from me
my family pressures me to get top marks
my parents want me to be a doctor but i don't
i'm scared to disappoint my parents
they compare me with my cousins
my parents only care about my grades
i can't choose my own subject
aama buwa le dherai pressure dinuhuncha
ghar ma padhai ko pressure cha
responses: Family expectations often come from love and worry, even when they feel heavy. A calm conversation about how you feel and what you're aiming for can help them understand you.
It may help to share your effort and your plan, not only your marks — parents often relax when they see you're taking things seriously.
If talking directly is hard, a teacher, counsellor or relative you trust might help explain your perspective.

patterns: i don't know what to do with my life
i don't know which subject to choose
i'm worried i won't get a job
i have no direction in life
what should i do after graduation
should i go abroad or stay in nepal
i feel lost about my future plans
responses: Feeling unsure about your path is normal at this stage. Try listing what you enjoy, what you're good at and what you value — overlaps can point to options.
Talking to people already working in fields you're curious about can make choices clearer. Small experiments like a short course or internship help too.
You don't need the whole plan now — just the next step. What's one thing you could explore this month?

patterns: i have nothing left to give
i don't care about my studies anymore
i've been working nonstop and i'm empty
i feel numb from too much work
i dread going to college every day
responses: Burnout often comes from long stress without enough recovery. Protecting rest — sleep, breaks and time off screens — is a priority, not a luxury.
Look for one thing you can reduce or say no to this week, and one restoring activity you can add, even for 15 minutes a day.
Lumora's Burnout Check can show how your recent mood, journaling and chats look together. It's indicative only, but it can help you notice patterns.

patterns: i wake up in the middle of the night
i only sleep a few hours
i stay up all night on my phone
i feel sleepy all day but can't sleep at night
i haven't slept properly in days
responses: A steady routine helps sleep: wake at the same time daily, avoid screens 30–60 minutes before bed, and keep caffeine to the morning.
If you can't sleep after about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm in dim light, then return to bed when sleepy. This helps your brain link bed with sleep.
Try a wind-down ritual: dim lights, a warm shower, slow breathing or a body-scan meditation. If sleep problems last for weeks, consider talking to a doctor.

patterns: i wake up scared from dreams
i'm afraid to sleep because of bad dreams
i dream about bad things happening
responses: Bad dreams are unsettling. After waking, ground yourself: turn on a soft light, notice your surroundings and breathe slowly until you feel settled.
A calm bedtime routine and writing down worries before bed can reduce nightmares for some people. If they're frequent or linked to something difficult that happened, a professional can help.

patterns: i eat too much when i'm stressed
i skip meals because of stress
my eating habits are messed up
i binge snack when i'm sad
responses: Stress often changes appetite. Try small, regular meals at set times, even if you're not hungry, and keep water and simple snacks nearby.
Noticing the link between feelings and eating is a good first step. If eating changes continue or worry you, please talk to a doctor or health professional.

patterns: my head hurts when i'm stressed
my stomach hurts when i'm nervous
i feel tightness in my chest when stressed
my jaw is clenched all the time
responses: Stress can show up in the body. Gentle stretching, warm showers and slow breathing can ease tension. Physical symptoms should also be checked by a doctor to rule out other causes.
Try progressive muscle relaxation: tense one muscle group for 5 seconds, then release, moving from your feet up to your face.

patterns: i'm having problems with my partner
my relationship is stressing me out
i feel unappreciated by my partner
i don't feel loved in my relationship
i'm not sure if i should stay in my relationship
my partner is jealous all the time
responses: Relationship conflict is draining. Try using 'I feel… when… because…' statements, which tend to cause less defensiveness than blame.
It may help to talk at a calm time, not mid-argument. Listen to understand, and agree on one small change each of you can try.
Healthy relationships should feel safe. If you ever feel controlled, threatened or hurt, please reach out to someone you trust or use the SOS page.

patterns: my boyfriend broke up with me
i can't get over my ex
i miss my ex so much
i still think about them every day
how do i move on after a breakup
responses: Heartbreak can feel physically painful. Let yourself grieve, keep simple routines going, and lean on friends or family.
Reducing contact — muting or unfollowing for a while — often helps healing. Each day without checking is progress.
It might help to write what you miss, what you don't miss, and what you learned. Over time the pain usually softens.

patterns: my parents fight all the time
i don't get along with my family
there's a lot of tension at home
i don't feel comfortable at home
my family is causing me stress
responses: Tension at home is really hard because it's hard to get away from. Having a calm space — your room, a library or a walk — can give you breathing room.
When talking with family, choose a calm moment and focus on how you feel rather than who's right. Sometimes a trusted relative can help mediate.
If you ever feel unsafe at home, please contact someone you trust or use the SOS page for help.

patterns: i had a fight with my best friend
i feel like my friends don't care
i don't fit in with my friend group
my friends talk behind my back
responses: Friendship hurts can be just as painful as other relationship problems. If it feels safe, an honest, calm conversation can clear up misunderstandings.
It's okay to invest more in friendships that feel mutual and kind. Meeting people through shared interests can widen your circle.
Give yourself time to feel hurt before deciding what to do. What would you like this friendship to look like?

patterns: i'm scared to talk in class
i get anxious in social situations
i'm too shy to make friends
i'm afraid people will judge me
i freeze when i have to present
responses: Social nerves often ease with gradual practice. Start small — asking a classmate a question or saying hi — and notice that it usually goes better than feared.
Before a social situation, slow breathing and a simple plan ('I'll ask one question') can lower anxiety. Focus on the other person rather than on yourself.
Most people are thinking about themselves far more than judging you. Be kind to yourself after each small step.

patterns: people at school make fun of me
my classmates tease me every day
someone keeps sending me mean messages
i'm scared to go to school because of bullies
responses: Bullying is never your fault. Keep a record of what happens (screenshots, dates) and tell a trusted teacher, family member or authority.
Online, you can block, report and save evidence. Talking to someone you trust can help you decide the next steps.
If you feel unsafe or threatened, please reach out for help right away — the SOS page lists places to contact.

patterns: i moved to a new city and feel alone
i'm living away from home and it's hard
i'm studying abroad and feel lonely
i want to go back home
responses: Homesickness is a sign of strong bonds. Regular calls with family, keeping familiar routines or foods, and slowly building new connections can help.
Exploring your new place a little at a time — a café, a park, a club — can help it start to feel like your own.

patterns: i hate the way i am
i feel like i'm not good enough
how do i build self confidence
i feel insecure all the time
responses: Harsh self-talk can feel true, but it isn't the full picture. Try writing down three things you did today, however small — it trains your mind to notice your strengths.
Ask yourself: would I speak to a friend this way? Try rephrasing one harsh thought into something kinder and more balanced.
Confidence grows through small kept promises. Set one tiny goal for today and notice when you complete it.

patterns: i don't feel like doing anything
i set goals but never follow through
i want to build good habits
responses: Motivation often comes after starting, not before. Pick something so small it's hard to say no to — five minutes, one page, one rep.
Connect goals to a reason you care about, and track small wins. Seeing progress is one of the strongest motivators.
Habit stacking can help: attach a new habit to something you already do, like reviewing notes right after dinner.

patterns: how do i take care of myself
how can i feel better today
what can i do to unwind
i want to look after my mental health
responses: Self-care can be simple: enough sleep, regular meals, some movement, time outside, and something you enjoy each day.
Try a small reset: put your phone down, have a glass of water, stretch for two minutes and take five slow breaths.
Make a short 'comfort list' of things that help — music, a walk, a call with a friend — so it's ready on hard days.

patterns: i compare my body to others online
responses: Many people struggle with how they see their bodies, especially with social media. Try noticing what your body does for you, not only how it looks.
Curating your feed — following accounts that make you feel good and muting those that don't — can make a real difference.
If worries about eating or your body are taking over daily life, please talk to a health professional; you deserve support.

patterns: i can't accept that they're gone
i miss my dad who died
how do i cope with loss
it's the anniversary of their death
responses: I'm so sorry for your loss. Grief has no right timeline, and it often comes in waves. Be gentle with yourself and let others support you.
Remembering them in a way that feels right — writing a letter, sharing a story, looking at photos — can help you carry the loss.
Keeping simple routines like eating and sleeping helps during grief. If the pain feels unmanageable for a long time, a counsellor can help.

patterns: how do i breathe to calm down
can we do a breathing exercise
i need to calm down quickly
responses: Let's try box breathing: breathe in for 4, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat 4 times, keeping your shoulders relaxed.
Try 4-7-8 breathing: in through your nose for 4, hold for 7, and breathe out slowly through your mouth for 8. Repeat 3–4 times.
Place a hand on your belly and breathe so it rises more than your chest. Slow, deep belly breaths tell your body it's safe.

patterns: i feel disconnected and need to ground
help me stay in the present
responses: Try 5-4-3-2-1 grounding: name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell and 1 you can taste.
A one-minute mindful pause: sit comfortably, notice your breath going in and out, and when your mind wanders, gently bring it back.
The Mindfulness page has guided audio exercises, like a body scan, that you can follow along with.

patterns: how do i handle my emotions
give me tips to feel better
how do i manage my feelings
what should i do when i feel bad
responses: Helpful coping tools include slow breathing, grounding, movement, journaling, talking to someone you trust, and planning small pleasant activities.
Try the 'name it to tame it' approach: put a name to what you feel ('I'm feeling anxious'). Naming emotions can reduce their intensity.
Make a coping plan: list 3 things that calm you, 2 people you can reach, and 1 place you feel safe.

patterns: what should i write in my journal
i want to write about my feelings
help me reflect on my day
responses: Here's a prompt: 'Right now I feel… because… What I need most is…' Write for five minutes without editing.
Try three lines tonight: one thing that was hard, one thing that went okay, and one thing you're grateful for.
You can use the Journal page to save entries with a mood tag and look back at patterns over time.

patterns: how do i find a counsellor
i want to talk to a psychiatrist
where can i get professional help
i think i need professional help
how do i talk to a counsellor
doctor sanga kura garna man lagyo
responses: Reaching out to a professional is a strong, healthy step. The Consultation page lets you book a slot with a psychiatrist, and your college may also have a counsellor.
If what you're feeling has lasted for weeks or is affecting your studies, sleep or relationships, talking to a mental health professional is a good idea.
It can help to write down what you've been experiencing before an appointment, so it's easier to explain.

patterns: i don't want to live anymore
i want to end my life
everyone would be better off without me
i have a plan to end it
i'm going to end it all
responses: I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. Your safety matters most right now. Please open the SOS page for Nepal helplines or contact local emergency services immediately, and tell someone you trust.

patterns: i hit myself when i'm upset
i scratch my skin until it bleeds
responses: Thank you for telling me — that takes courage. Your safety comes first. Please use the SOS page to contact a helpline or emergency services now, and reach out to someone you trust.

patterns: i drink to forget my problems
i take pills to feel better
my friends pressure me to drink
responses: Using alcohol or substances to cope is common, but it often makes stress and low mood worse over time. Notice when and why you use, and try replacing one occasion with another coping activity.

Cutting down is easier with support. A doctor or counsellor can help confidentially — you don't have to manage it alone. If you ever take something in a dangerous amount, seek emergency help immediately.
